question: Our baby missed the six-week vaccines because of illness. Should we restart all vaccines?
answer:
No, you don't need to restart. If a dose is late, the series is simply continued from where it stands, and the earlier doses are not repeated (INDIA-UIP, p. 15). The 6-week vaccines (bOPV, Pentavalent, Rota, fIPV, PCV) can still be given later. Pentavalent, Rota, fIPV and PCV can be given up to 1 year of age, and bOPV up to 5 years (INDIA-UIP, p. 7). Rota, Penta and OPV need a gap of at least 4 weeks between doses (INDIA-UIP, p. 15).

A child with mild fever, diarrhoea or malnutrition can still be vaccinated. If the baby was critically ill and needed hospital care, vaccination can wait until the baby is stable (INDIA-UIP, p. 20).

Please take your baby's vaccination card to your doctor or the nearest vaccination centre soon so they can plan the catch-up. If the baby is unwell now, please contact your doctor.

question: Is it okay to drink coffee while pregnant?
answer: Yes, you can usually have some coffee, but it helps to keep your caffeine low. WHO recommends that women with a high daily caffeine intake (more than 300 mg a day) cut down, to lower the risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight (WHO-ANC, p. 38). Caffeine is also in tea, cola, chocolate and some over-the-counter medicines, so it all adds up. A cup of instant coffee has about 60 mg, but some commercially brewed coffees have more than 150 mg per serving (WHO-ANC, p. 38). Black or green tea usually has under 50 mg per 250 mL (WHO-ANC, p. 38). So one or two small cups of instant coffee a day would stay well under 300 mg, but a couple of large café coffees could go over. The evidence suggests low intake (under 150 mg a day) was not linked to more pregnancy loss (WHO-ANC, p. 39). Please check with your doctor about what is right for you.

question: My wife is 8 weeks pregnant. What should I do as a first-time father?
answer:
Congratulations! At 8 weeks, here is how you can help:

• Registration: Her pregnancy should be registered within 12 weeks, with the first antenatal check-up in the first trimester (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7; p. 9). Going along with her is a good first step.
• Regular visits: Plan for at least four antenatal visits, with blood and urine tests, blood pressure and weight checked each time (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7).
• Medicines: She should not take any medicine in the first trimester unless a doctor advises it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7).
• Support: Husbands and families are encouraged to support her through pregnancy, delivery and after birth (MOHFW-ANC, p. 9).
• Intimacy: Sex is generally safe in an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her desire may dip, which is normal, so always ask for her consent and see to her comfort (MOHFW-ANC, p. 33). Check with her doctor if there are any risks.
• Plan ahead: Antenatal visits are also the time to make a birth plan and be ready for emergencies (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7).

If she has bleeding or severe pain, please contact her doctor or go to the hospital right away.

question: How can I make a hospital emergency plan before my wife goes into labour?
answer:

1. Know your nearest facilities: find the nearest PHC with 24-hour emergency care and the FRU, which has blood transfusion and surgery (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
2. Choose the place of delivery and who will conduct it, and identify a referral facility and how you'd get there (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27).
3. Arrange transport in advance (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27).
4. Line up support people for other children or household tasks, and plan to accompany your wife (MOHFW-ANC, pp. 29, 89).
5. Estimate delivery and transport costs, keep an emergency fund, and check schemes like JSY (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
6. Keep the Maternal and Child Protection Card and any JSY/BPL papers handy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27).
7. Agree on who does what in an emergency, and learn the danger signs. If any appear, go to the PHC/FRU at once, day or night (MOHFW-ANC, pp. 29, 90).

Please also ask your doctor which hospital and danger signs apply to your wife's situation.

question: How do I change a newborn diaper and know if the baby has enough wet diapers?
answer:

For wet diapers: an exclusively breastfed baby who is getting enough milk usually passes dilute urine at least 6-8 times in 24 hours. Passing concentrated, dark yellow or strong-smelling urine fewer than 6 times a day (often fewer than 4) suggests not enough milk (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 121). This check is not reliable if the baby gets other drinks. Weight gain is the most reliable sign: at least 500 g a month, or about 125 g a week (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 121).

If your baby has fewer wet diapers than this, or seems unwell, please contact your doctor soon.

question: Which iron-rich foods can I eat as a vegetarian?
answer: Good question, and well done for thinking about iron at 24 weeks. As a vegetarian, you can include: green leafy vegetables (spinach, amaranth, fenugreek, drumstick leaves), pulses and whole pulses like dals, beans and chickpeas, dry fruits and raisins, and jaggery (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 147). Iron from plants is absorbed less well, so a few tips help: eat vitamin C fruits like guava, orange, lemon or papaya with meals; use fermented and sprouted foods like idli, dosa and sprouted pulses; and keep tea and coffee about 2 hours away from meals and iron tablets (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36; INDIA-JSSK, p. 28). Cooking in iron pots may also help (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 147). Food alone may not be enough, so daily iron and folic acid (IFA) tablets are advised in pregnancy (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Please ask your doctor about the right tablets for you.

question: I follow a Jain diet. How can I get enough protein while pregnant?
answer:
Good news: a Jain diet can meet protein needs with planning. At week 18 you need about 8g extra protein a day, rising to 18g in the third trimester (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 31). Here is what the sources suggest:

- Combine cereals and pulses; good quality protein comes from cereals and pulses in about a 3:1 ratio, plus milk (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).
- A dish like paushtik khichari mixes rice, dal and vegetables, with a little ghee (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
- Eat dal or chana daily, with nuts, oilseeds and milk or curd. The sample chart includes 20g nuts, pulses and milk (ICMR-NIN-DG, pp. 33-34).
- Eat 5-6 smaller meals a day if large meals are hard (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
- Have green leafy vegetables daily, and vitamin C fruits like guava or orange to help iron absorption (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34).

I don't have a trusted source for the rest of your Jain restrictions, such as root vegetables, or for supplements. Please ask your doctor or a dietitian for a personal plan and about iron and folic acid tablets.

question: Do I need to eat more in the third trimester?
answer: Yes, a little more, but not double. For a woman of normal weight, the second and third trimesters need about 350 extra calories a day, and about 18 g extra protein in the third trimester (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 31). If you are undernourished, about 100 more calories a day is advised (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 33). The extra should come from nourishing foods like dal, vegetables, milk, nuts, eggs, fish or meat if you eat them, and fruit, not from highly processed or high-fat, sugar and salt foods (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). If big meals are hard, eat 5-6 smaller meals a day, with green leafy vegetables daily. Iron and folic acid tablets and iodized salt are also advised (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Your doctor can tell you how much weight gain is right for you and whether your tablets need any change. Would you like some easy meal ideas?

question: What should I eat while breastfeeding?
answer: Congratulations on feeding your baby. Breastfeeding needs a little extra nourishment. In the first six months you need about 600 extra calories and 13.6 g extra protein a day, and about 520 extra calories and 10.6 g protein in the next six months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Eat a variety of foods: cereals with pulses, milk, seasonal vegetables including green leafy ones, and fresh fruit. Since you eat eggs, they are a good source of protein and iron, and eggs can replace some of the pulses (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Vitamin C foods like guava or oranges with meals help iron absorption. Try to avoid highly processed foods high in fat, sugar and salt (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Most women simply eat to appetite, but variety matters (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 178). Avoid tobacco and alcohol, and take medicines only on a doctor's advice (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 42). Lactating women are advised daily iron and folic acid supplements, so please ask your doctor about these (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).

question: Why do doctors give iron and folic acid tablets in pregnancy?
answer: Pregnancy asks a lot from your body, so doctors give iron and folic acid to protect you and your baby. Iron and folic acid are both needed to make haemoglobin and prevent anaemia (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Iron also supports your baby's brain development, and low iron in pregnancy can lower birth weight (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). WHO says daily iron and folic acid helps prevent maternal anaemia, infection after birth, low birth weight and preterm birth (WHO-ANC, p. 23). Folic acid also helps prevent neural tube defects (WHO-ANC, p. xi). Nausea, constipation and black stools are common and not serious (MOHFW-ANC, p. 25). Tea can block iron absorption, so avoid it around the tablet (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Please take the tablets exactly as your doctor has prescribed, and ask them about any side-effects that bother you. Iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables, pulses and fish also help.

question: I eat idli, dosa and sambar every day. How can I make my pregnancy meals more balanced?
answer:
Idli, dosa and sambar are a good base, since cereals and pulses together give energy and protein. To balance them, the guidelines suggest a wide variety of foods each day. Here are some easy additions:

• Add vegetables and greens: try vegetable idli or dosa, or methi or palak roti (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34). Aim for green leafy vegetables daily, as they are a good source of iron (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
• Add fruit: 1-2 servings daily, with vitamin C fruits like guava or orange to help iron absorption (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177; ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 34).
• Add milk or curd, and a few nuts or seeds (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 33).
• If you eat eggs, fish or meat, a portion of dal can be swapped for them (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).
• Mix two cereals, or cereal with pulses, and add vegetables.
• Eat 5-6 smaller meals if that suits you better (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
• Use iodized salt (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).

In the second trimester, about 350 extra kcal a day is advised (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 33). For iron or other supplements, please ask your doctor.

question: Can I eat fish during pregnancy in coastal Karnataka?

Fish or chicken is preferred over red or organ meat (INDIA-JSSK, p. 30). The same guidelines say there is no need to avoid specific foods because of food beliefs or taboos (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 35). Food safety matters most: avoid contaminated food, which can cause food-borne illness (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 35). Spinach, bathua, amaranth and mustard greens are listed (INDIA-JSSK, p. 21). Pulses, dal, legumes, groundnuts, ragi and jaggery are also recommended (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177; MOHFW-ANC, p. 30). Dry fruits contain iron too (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Try methi or palak roti, or a paushtik khichari with rice, dal and greens.

Plant iron is absorbed less well, so add vitamin C fruits like guava, orange or lemon (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Guava is usually affordable. Avoid tea or coffee before, during or within an hour after meals, because they block iron absorption (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36; MOHFW-ANC, p. 30).

Iron and folic acid tablets are recommended from week 12 (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 36). Your ANM or Anganwadi can guide you on these and on supplementary nutrition.

question: My mother says drinking saffron milk makes the baby fair. Is that true?
answer: I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor. None of the passages I have say anything about saffron milk or about it changing a baby's skin colour, so I can't confirm it. What I can say is that the library does list many common beliefs as myths (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80-81). Your baby's skin tone is not something food choices are shown to change in these sources. If you enjoy saffron milk as a warm treat, please check with your doctor that it suits you and your diet in pregnancy. It's lovely that your mother is caring for you; you can thank her and still lean on your doctor's advice.

question: What should I ask during my first ultrasound appointment?
answer:
Congratulations on reaching your first scan! My trusted library has no ready-made list of questions for an ultrasound, but it does explain what an early scan is for. WHO recommends one scan before 24 weeks to estimate gestational age, help detect fetal anomalies and multiple pregnancies, and improve your pregnancy experience (WHO-ANC, p. 58). You could ask:
- Will the scan confirm my due date and how many babies there are?
- What will you be checking, and when will I get the report?
- Who will explain the results to me, and what happens next if something needs a follow-up?

Also be ready to share your last period date, which helps work out the due date (MOHFW-ANC, p. 13), and any complications from earlier pregnancies (MOHFW-ANC, p. 15). I can't interpret scan results, so please go over them with your doctor. For anything else about the scan, I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor.

question: Do I need Td vaccination during pregnancy in India?
answer: Yes, Td is part of routine care in pregnancy in India (INDIA-UIP, p. 3). At 20 weeks, you're in good time. Td-1 is given as early as possible in pregnancy, and Td-2 follows 4 weeks later. Td-2 or a booster is preferably given before 36 weeks (INDIA-UIP, p. 5). If you already had two doses of Td/TT in a previous pregnancy within the last 3 years, you need only one dose or booster (INDIA-UIP, p. 5; MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). It is given in the upper arm, and mild swelling, pain or redness for a day or two can happen (MOHFW-ANC, p. 26). I can't see your vaccination records, so please tell your doctor or ANM which Td/TT doses you've had before, and they'll confirm what you need.

question: My glucose test was flagged high. Can I fix gestational diabetes by avoiding rice completely?
answer: I'm sorry the result was flagged; that's worrying, but GDM is manageable. Cutting out rice completely isn't what the guidelines advise. They say total carbohydrate should be controlled and spread across 3 small meals and 2-3 snacks, with lower glycemic index carbohydrates emphasised (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29). Refined carbs like sweets, juices and table sugar should be avoided (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29). Fibre-rich foods like whole grains, whole pulses, beans, non-starchy vegetables and whole fruit help control blood sugar, and fried foods are best avoided (INDIA-JSSK, p. 29-30). Walking 30 minutes twice a day is encouraged (INDIA-JSSK, p. 30). Diet is only one part: GDM needs regular glucose monitoring and treatment, and a meal plan should be set with a specialist (INDIA-JSSK, p. 30). Treatment is effective at reducing risks (WHO-ANC, p. 48). Please see your doctor soon to confirm the diagnosis and get a plan made for you. I can't say whether diet alone will be enough; that is for your doctor to judge.

question: Can I take an overnight bus at 36 weeks to go to my parents house for delivery?
answer:
I'm glad you're planning ahead. The passages I have don't say whether an overnight bus at 36 weeks is safe, so I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor before you travel, and ask for a written summary of your antenatal records to carry with you.

What the sources do tell me: complications can develop at any time and aren't always predictable, so delivering at a health facility with staff and a referral system is recommended (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). Labour before 37 weeks counts as pre-term, and the baby may need specialised newborn care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 81). So it helps to know which facility near your parents' home you'll use, and how far it is.

If you leak fluid, have bleeding, fever, or regular pains at any point, contact your doctor or go to the nearest hospital straight away. Please speak to your doctor about your travel plan soon.

question: I feel anxious about labour and everyone says I should just be happy.
answer: Feeling anxious about labour is very common, and you don't have to simply "be happy" on cue. Your feelings are valid. Here is what my trusted source says that may help. Skilled birth attendants are expected to give emotional support as well as physical care during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can choose the position that feels comfortable to you (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39), and you can eat and drink as you wish during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). Your carers should explain what they are doing and ask your consent before a vaginal examination (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). Talking with your doctor or midwife about your birth plan and fears may ease your mind. I don't have a trusted source for treating anxiety itself, so please ask your doctor. If the worry feels overwhelming, stops you sleeping or eating, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your doctor now.

question: My neighbour gave me herbal kadha for contractions. Should I take it?
answer: Please don't start the kadha yet. At 32 weeks, contractions are not something to treat at home, and I don't have a trusted source saying any herbal kadha is safe in pregnancy. Please ask your doctor. The passages I have only cover postpartum cramps, not contractions before birth (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 32). They also say women often turn to herbal remedies for common symptoms (WHO-ANC, p. 76), so you're not alone in wondering. Regular or painful contractions at 32 weeks can be a sign of early labour. Please call your doctor or go to the hospital now, and say what you've been given. Also tell them if you notice leaking fluid, bleeding, or less baby movement. If you still have the kadha, keep the packet or ingredient list to show them. I can't see what's in it, so I can't say whether it's safe.

question: I had a C-section. How should I plan help at home in the first two weeks?
answer: Congratulations, and well done on your recovery. The passages don't give a ready-made home-help schedule, but here is what they support. Plan for care contacts: WHO recommends a postnatal check between 48 and 72 hours, another between 7 and 14 days, and one at week six (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). A home visit in the first week by a skilled health worker is recommended, or an outpatient visit if that isn't feasible (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 173). Plan for food: after a C-section you need energy, and calories shouldn't be restricted for long. Fluids are encouraged, about 2-3 litres a day including milk, unless your surgeon says otherwise (INDIA-JSSK, p. 10). So a helper for meals and fluids is useful. Plan for emotional support: many women feel unprepared for pain and discomfort and for postpartum low mood (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 91), so line up someone to talk to. I don't have a trusted source for activity limits, lifting or wound care. Please ask your doctor. If you have heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain or wound problems, contact your doctor or go to the hospital now.

question: My mother-in-law suggests giving honey to my newborn before breastfeeding.
answer: Please don't give honey or any other drink or food before breastfeeding. Trusted guidance says to avoid honey, glucose or water before breastfeeding starts and at any time in the first 6 months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Feeds given before the first breastfeed can delay milk flow and make the baby ill (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). They may also not be hygienic and can cause intestinal infections and diarrhoea (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Colostrum, your first milk, is all most babies need at first. It is rich in antibodies and vitamin A and protects against infection (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 19). For the first six months, breast milk alone gives all the food and water your baby needs (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). You could kindly tell your mother-in-law that the doctors and nurses advise only breast milk for now, and that her love will show in helping you rest and feed. If your baby is not feeding well, please talk to your doctor or nurse.

question: I feel I have too little milk on day three. Should I switch to formula?
answer: Worrying about milk on day three is very common, and you're not alone. Please don't switch to formula just yet. Colostrum (the milk in the first 3-4 days) comes in small amounts, and a newborn's stomach is tiny (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). Most mothers can make enough milk if the baby suckles often and well (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Frequent feeding, including at night, and good attachment help build supply, and bottles or other feeds can reduce it (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123; p. 127). The reliable signs of too little milk are poor weight gain and fewer than 6 wet urines a day, with dark, strong-smelling urine (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 121). That is mainly for older babies, so ask your doctor, nurse or a lactation counsellor to watch a feed and check your baby's weight and wet nappies. If your baby seems very sleepy, won't feed, or has hardly any wet nappies, contact your doctor or go to the hospital now.

question: My family wants me to eat only rice and rasam after delivery. Is that enough?
answer: Rice and rasam on their own are unlikely to be enough. After delivery your body needs energy and a variety of foods, and a breastfeeding mother needs about 600 extra calories a day from different foods (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Mixing cereal with pulses and vegetables, such as a khichri with green leafy vegetables and a little ghee, covers many needs in one dish (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). The hospital sample menus include milk, dal, eggs, vegetables, curd and fruit alongside roti or rice (INDIA-JSSK, p. 20). Drink at least 2 litres of safe water a day, including soups, milk and buttermilk (INDIA-JSSK, p. 11). You can keep rice and rasam as part of your meals, and respect family tradition by adding dal, vegetables, curd and fruit. If you had a C-section, your surgeon decides how your diet progresses (INDIA-JSSK, p. 10). For advice specific to you, please ask your doctor.

question: Can I give water to my two-month-old in Bengaluru summer?
answer: No, you don't need to give water to your two-month-old, even in Bengaluru's summer. Breastmilk has all the water a baby needs, and exclusively breastfed babies need no water for the first 6 months, even in hot weather (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Giving water can reduce how much milk your baby takes and raises the risk of diarrhoea (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 39). In hot weather, just feed on demand, whenever your baby asks (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32), and dress your baby in 1-2 light layers (MOHFW-ANC, p. 53). If your baby seems unusually drowsy, feeds poorly, or has very few wet nappies, please contact your doctor right away. You're doing a lovely job.
